text: Authentication answers one question: are you who you claim to be? Every method for answering it falls into one of three factor categories, and once you know those three categories, multi-factor authentication stops feeling like a random extra step and starts making obvious sense.

Something you know is a memorized secret — a password, a PIN, a security question answer. It's the weakest factor alone, because it can be phished, guessed, or reused from a site that's already been breached. Something you have is a physical object you currently hold, like your phone or a hardware key, which an attacker on the other side of the world typically doesn't. Something you are is a biometric trait, like a fingerprint or your face, which can't be memorized or handed off. Real multi-factor authentication combines factors from different categories, not two things from the same one, because two knowledge-based secrets don't add any real independent protection.

An authenticator app generates a new six-digit code every 30 seconds, computed on the device itself, which makes it strong. SMS codes are convenient but carry real weaknesses — SIM swapping, where an attacker ports your number to their own SIM, and interception on the aging SS7 network, which is why NIST treats SMS as a restricted method. A hardware key like a YubiKey ties its cryptographic check to the real site's domain, which makes it effectively phishing-resistant.

Picture logging into a bank. You type your password — something you know — and it's correct, but the bank doesn't log you in yet. It also asks for the code currently showing in your authenticator app — something you have. Only when both check out does the session open. An attacker who phished your password alone is stuck right there, because stealing a password no longer equals taking over the account.
That's authentication: proving who you are. Next up, authorization — once you're logged in, what are you actually allowed to do? We'll compare three real models: RBAC, DAC, and MAC.
